sections.body: The survey begins from a concrete systems pressure: VR applications require real-time responses while scenes become more expensive to render. The 13 ms latency tolerance and the observation that delayed content can conflict with user interaction ground the problem in perception rather than only hardware throughput. This makes foveated rendering a practical response to a user-experience constraint.
sections.heading: Performance Motivation

sections.body: The core mechanism is asymmetric human visual sensitivity. The source explains that the fovea supports clear central vision, while peripheral regions can tolerate reduced quality. Visual acuity and contrast sensitivity models turn that biological fact into rendering rules, indicating where spatial, temporal, luminance, or chromatic detail can be reduced with limited perceptual cost.
sections.heading: Perceptual Mechanism

sections.body: The paper does not treat foveated rendering as one technique. It frames the area as a combination of perceptual modeling, multi-quality regional rendering, and integration into renderer architectures. This framing is useful because a method can fail by using the wrong perception model, by choosing poor quality falloff, or by being incompatible with the rendering pipeline it is supposed to accelerate.
sections.heading: Three Design Problems

sections.body: The taxonomy is the survey's organizing contribution. By classifying methods by data type, foveation principle, and rendering paradigm, it connects design decisions to implementation contexts. The categories also prevent overly narrow comparisons: a technique for mesh rasterization, volume ray casting, hologram phase retrieval, or 360-degree video transmission may all be foveated, but they solve different engineering problems.
sections.heading: Taxonomy Contribution

sections.body: The application of the taxonomy to 90 reports from 1990 to 2021 gives the survey more than a conceptual structure. It functions as a map of the literature, separating early approaches from the more recent decade and showing how methods diversified across data representations, principles, and renderer types as hardware and application needs changed.
sections.heading: Historical Coverage

sections.body: The source is careful about evaluation limits. Existing objective metrics such as FSNR, FWQI, FMSE, and WSSIM each omit or assume important perceptual factors, such as spatio-temporal contrast sensitivity, fixation position, or saliency-model accuracy. That means performance gains alone are not enough; comparability depends on better perceptual metrics and datasets.
sections.heading: Limits and Assumptions

sections.body: For designers, the practical message is that foveated rendering should be chosen and evaluated as a system-level tradeoff among perception, data representation, rendering algorithm, display hardware, and task. The open problems around AR fusion, holograms, light fields, gaze prediction, AI reconstruction, and task guidance suggest that the field remains active even where core VR mesh and volume concepts are mature.
sections.heading: Practical Interpretation

source_dossier.summary_long: The source is a broad survey of foveated rendering, centered on the idea that VR and related interactive graphics systems cannot simply render every part of every scene at maximum quality when scene complexity and human latency tolerance are both severe constraints. The paper motivates the field with the increasing cost of rendering diverse materials, dynamic objects, and complex physical phenomena, and with the approximately 13 ms visual-latency tolerance discussed in its introduction. Against that background, foveated rendering is presented as a perceptual allocation strategy: render the foveal region at high quality, render peripheral regions at lower quality, and rely on human visual-system limits so that the user does not perceive unacceptable loss. The survey's argument is structured around three problems that any foveated method must solve: it must use an appropriate perceptual model, decide how quality varies across regions, and fit that decision into a concrete rendering paradigm. The perceptual discussion emphasizes visual acuity and contrast sensitivity models, including spatial, temporal, luminance, chromatic, and binocular considerations. The taxonomy then turns those concerns into a practical classification with three axes: input data type, foveation principle, and rendering paradigm. This lets the paper compare work on image/video, volumes, meshes, point clouds, holograms, and light fields, as well as principles such as multi-spatial resolution, multi-temporal resolution, multi-luminance resolution, multi-color resolution, and level of detail. The rendering-paradigm axis includes rasterization, ray tracing, ray casting, instant radiosity, shadow mapping, simplification, neural rendering, photon mapping, phase retrieval, and data transmission. By applying the taxonomy to 90 reports from 1990 to 2021, the survey presents the field as mature in some areas, especially volume data and geometric meshes, but still unresolved in others. Its discussion highlights open problems in broader use of human visual features, AI-assisted gaze and reconstruction methods, emerging data types such as holograms and light fields, objective quality metrics, AR fusion constraints, and task-oriented uses beyond speed improvement alone.
source_dossier.summary_short: This survey presents foveated rendering as a response to the real-time burden of complex VR scenes and the perceptual consequences of latency. It explains how human visual-system models let renderers concentrate fidelity near gaze while reducing work in peripheral regions. Its main contribution is a taxonomy organized by data type, foveation principle, and rendering paradigm, applied to 90 reports from 1990 to 2021.

summary: Wang, Shi, and Liu survey foveated rendering as a perceptually grounded acceleration strategy for VR and related display systems. The source frames the field around HVS perceptual models, regional quality variation, and integration into rendering paradigms, then proposes a three-dimensional taxonomy and applies it to 90 reports from 1990 to 2021.
